My most recent pre-print, "Exploiting Exact Conditionals Improves Conditioning: Provably Fast Mixing Time Bounds By Sampling from the Marginal", has finally[^1] been completed and uploaded to ArXiv!
I really loved writing this paper and I felt like I went out of my comfort zone to do it.

[^1]: ε-(´∀`;) 

It began at [ICERM](https://icerm.brown.edu).
My postdoc superviser, [Dr. Elizabeth Newman](https://elizabethnewman.owlstown.net), and I were invited for a semester long program for the Spring 2026 alongside many other great mathematicians.
This paper began as a collaboration between us, [Dr. Julianne Chung](https://www.math.emory.edu/~jmchung/) and [Dr. Federica Milinanni](https://sites.google.com/view/federicamilinanni).
All very excellent mathematicians, and I think the largest group I've worked with for a single paper.

To give some background, Liz and I have been working on some modern applications and implications of the classical optimization technique variable projection.
Consider the optimization problem
\[
  \min_{\theta \in \Theta} F(\theta).
\]
In reality, $\theta$ is usually partitioned into multiple sub-blocks of variables.
If you imagine a fully connected neural network, $\theta$ breaks up into the individual layers' weights and biases.
In such a construction, there might exist variables that are 'easier' to optimize out than others.
In particular, suppose I isolate out a block of variables $w$, and rewrite my function in the form
\[
  F:\mathcal W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R,
  \qquad
  w\in\mathcal W\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_w},
  \quad
  \theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\theta}.
\]
Then, I can consider the joint problem
\[
  \min_{w,\theta} F(w,\theta).
\]
Variable projection separates this into the inner problem
\[
  \mathcal W_\star(\theta)
  :=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{w\in\mathcal W}F(w,\theta),
  \qquad
  w_\star(\theta)\in\mathcal W_\star(\theta),
\]
and the outer problem
\[
  \min_{\theta\in\Theta}\phi(\theta),
  \qquad
  \phi(\theta)
  :=\min_{w\in\mathcal W}F(w,\theta)
  =F(w_\star(\theta),\theta).
\]
That is, now we're optimizing solely over $\theta$ and, at each evaluation, we solve an inner problem for $w_\star$.
But why?
Well, it turns out that the explicit elimination of this block confers a conditioning advantage to the underlying optimization problem.

---

::: {#thm-variable-projection-conditioning}
## Conditioning under variable projection

Suppose that $F$ is twice continuously differentiable and that
$\bar w=w_\star(\bar\theta)$ is an interior solution of the inner problem.
Write the full Hessian at $(\bar w,\bar\theta)$ as
\[
  H=\nabla^2F
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
    A & B\\
    B^\mathsf T & D
  \end{bmatrix},
  \qquad
  A=\nabla^2_{ww}F,
  \quad B=\nabla^2_{w\theta}F,
  \quad D=\nabla^2_{\theta\theta}F.
\]
If $H\succ0$, then the stationarity equation $\nabla_wF=0$ determines a
continuously differentiable local branch $w_\star(\theta)$ of strict inner
minimizers through $(\bar w,\bar\theta)$. For the corresponding local reduced
objective $\phi(\theta)=F(w_\star(\theta),\theta)$, the reduced Hessian is the
Schur complement
\[
  \nabla^2\phi(\bar\theta)
  =D-B^\mathsf T A^{-1}B=:S,
\]
and
\[
  \lambda_{\min}(H)\leq\lambda_{\min}(S),
  \qquad
  \lambda_{\max}(S)\leq\lambda_{\max}(H).
\]
Consequently,
\[
  \kappa_2\!\left(\nabla^2\phi(\bar\theta)\right)
  =\kappa_2(S)
  \leq\kappa_2(H)
  =\kappa_2\!\left(\nabla^2F(w_\star(\bar\theta),\bar\theta)\right).
\]
:::

---

If the optimization problem for $w_\star$ is easy, then the expense of needing to crush it can be negligable in favor of the per-iteration improvement during optimization.
Both Liz and I have written a series of papers investigating this.
